Paragraph:
Translation: There are also great, heroic, powerful fighters like Dhrstaketu, Cekitana, Kasiraja, Purujit, Kuntibhoja and Saibya. 

Purport: [No purport provided for this verse in the source text].
Situation/Problem_Faced: Duryodhana continues his obsessive enumeration of the powerful and heroic kings and warriors assembled on the opposing side, highlighting his mounting internal anxiety regarding the enemy's vast strength.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: By listing these additional formidable fighters, Duryodhana further emphasizes the gravity of the threat to his commander, Dronacarya, ensuring no enemy is underestimated.
Outcome/Resolution: The psychological pressure within Duryodhana builds as he mentally reinforces the strength and depth of the enemy alliance, feeding his own paranoia.

Spiritual_Psychological_Concept_Indian.Concept: Bhaya (Existential fear stemming from a reliance on material alliances rather than divine will)
Ajnana (Ignorance; calculating victory purely based on material counting rather than righteousness)

Brief_Summary_Spiritual: The text continues to reveal the fragmented and fearful consciousness of one disconnected from dharma. Duryodhana evaluates the impending conflict purely through the lens of material strength, alliances, and numbers, completely missing the spiritual reality of the battlefield.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Duryodhana displays signs of psychological rumination. By continuously reciting the names of powerful adversaries, he feeds his own anxiety, spiraling further into a state of distress. This hyper-focus on perceived external threats is a common cognitive distortion when an individual feels fundamentally insecure about their position.
